newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli closure raises Palestinian unemployment.
newsitem.headline: Israeli closure raises Palestinian unemployment.

text.p: Palestinian officials on Tuesday blamed a protracted Israeli closure of the West Bank and Gaza Strip for high unemployment that has left one in five Palestinians without work.

"As a result of the closure the existing high unemployment rate has reached astronomic levels and is considered among the highest in the world," said Hassan Abu Libdeh, head of the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics (PCBS).
Abu Libdeh said that according to a PCBS survey carried out in February, the unemployment rate stood at 19.5 percent in Gaza and the West Bank including Arab East Jerusalem.
This was calculated from 106,275 people being without work out of a labour force of 545,000.
Breaking the figures down into areas, Abu Libdeh said: "Of the labour force in the West Bank, 17.7 percent are unemployed while in the Gaza Strip 24.1 percent are unemployed."

"The unemployment rate increased by 40 percent in Gaza and 17 percent in the West Bank after the recent closures," he told reporters. "In Gaza, out of every 10 eligible workers, only one has the chance to find a job."

Israel has periodically sealed off the West Bank and Gaza since parts of those areas came under Palestinian rule in 1994 under a PLO-Israeli peace deal. Israel has tightened the closure after Moslem suicide bombings.

The closure prevents thousands of Palestinian workers from reaching their jobs in Israel. Palestinian officials call the closures "collective punishment" which is suffocating an already ailing economy.

They said before the 1994 closure more than 60,000 people were employed in Israel compared to less than 5,000 now. An Israeli army spokeswoman said 10,000 people in Gaza, with the proper permits, were allowed to work in Israel.
"Even when Israel announces the easing of the closure it takes measures to prevent many people from reaching their jobs in Israel," Abu Libdeh said.
Israel tightened its closure of the West Bank on April 15 citing warnings of "terrorist" attacks.
Abu Libdeh complained that 27.3 percent of Palestinians were underpaid, earning less than $300 a month.
He said unemployment among women had risen because men had been forced to compete for jobs traditionally done by women, such as in the textile industry.
